previous.explanation_en: 杀 is a verb meaning to cause someone or an animal to die. By itself, it does not specify the motive or method.

sources.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 殺
sources.summary_en: The CUHK character database records 殺 as meaning killing in bronze inscriptions and classical examples. It reports differing scholarly interpretations of an oracle-bone form proposed as an ancestor: Chen Jian identifies it as an early form of 殺 with a killing sense, while Liu Yun proposes that it meant striking. It also records other uses, including decline or withering, fighting, and degree intensification.

sources.title: 說文解字「殺」 - 「說文解字」在線查詢
sources.summary_en: The page gives the Shuowen entry 殺：戮也。从殳，杀聲 and reproduces Duan Yucai’s note. The entry records an analysis of the graph’s components and a gloss equating 殺 with 戮; it does not establish how the modern word’s meaning developed.

sources.title: 殺 shā - 汉典
sources.summary_en: The dictionary defines the relevant sense as causing a person or animal to lose life and gives classical examples. It lists distinct senses such as fighting, withering, and postverbal degree intensification. Its detailed graph-origin account differs in emphasis from the CUHK database’s presentation of competing proposals.

claims.text_en: In the supplied examples, 杀 is a verb meaning to kill: it describes intended or completed killing of people. The wording does not specify a legal status, motive, or method except where a sentence explicitly mentions a weapon.

The Shuowen entry glosses 殺 as 戮 and records the analysis 从殳、杀聲. This is an account of the traditional graph structure; it does not show that the modern verb is compositionally built from independently meaningful word parts.

The CUHK database reports competing interpretations of an oracle-bone form proposed as an early form of 殺: one identifies it as an ancestor with a killing sense, while another assigns it the sense ‘strike.’ The database describes the bronze form as adding 人 to a simplified version of that earlier form and identifies its meaning as killing. These proposals concern character history and do not by themselves establish a derivation of the modern word’s meaning from the parts of simplified 杀.
The sources record other uses of 殺, including fighting, withering or decline, and degree intensification. Those uses are distinct from the direct ‘kill’ sense in the supplied examples.

The graph-history accounts are not fully aligned: the CUHK page reports competing interpretations of the early form, whereas 汉典’s detailed explanation presents a killing interpretation for an oracle-bone form. The opened sources do not resolve that disagreement or establish a complete historical derivation of the modern word.
